title: IBM to Acquire HRL Laboratories to Expand Quantum Roadmap with Silicon-Spin Qubits - Quantum Computing Report
gist: IBM (NYSE: IBM) signed a definitive agreement to acquire HRL Laboratories — the Malibu R&D institution jointly owned by Boeing and General Motors — adding silicon-spin qubits as a second hardware modality alongside superconducting circuits. Financial terms were not disclosed; the deal is expected to close by the end of Q3 2026, and Boeing and GM will stay on as IBM quantum-application partners.

insights.claim: IBM has signed a definitive agreement to acquire HRL Laboratories, LLC, the Malibu-based R&D institution jointly owned by Boeing and General Motors, with financial terms not disclosed.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Undisclosed terms mean the price signal for spin-qubit IP stays hidden — but Boeing and GM divesting a crown-jewel lab is itself a portfolio-strategy datapoint for both.
insights.locator: IBM (NYSE: IBM) has signed a definitive agreement

insights.claim: The IBM-HRL transaction is expected to close by the end of the third quarter of 2026, subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: A dated close gives a concrete event to track; a defense-adjacent lab changing hands invites regulatory scrutiny that could slip the timeline.
insights.quote: The transaction is expected to close by the end of the third quarter of 2026, subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals.
insights.locator: Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed

insights.claim: Following the transaction, Boeing and General Motors will continue partnering with IBM to develop quantum applications and advanced industrial workloads, converting former owners into anchor customers.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: IBM buys the lab and keeps two blue-chip industrial application partners — a low-cost route to enterprise quantum use cases in aerospace and automotive.
insights.quote: Following the transaction, both Boeing and GM will continue partnering with IBM to develop quantum applications and advanced industrial workloads.
insights.locator: IBM (NYSE: IBM) has signed a definitive agreement

insights.claim: IBM is adding silicon-spin qubits as a parallel path to fault tolerance alongside its historically superconducting-centered hardware roadmap, making it a dual-modality quantum hardware player.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Modality diversification hedges IBM against a superconducting dead-end and pressures pure-play single-modality quantum companies.
insights.locator: Adding a Dual-Track Modality via Silicon Fabrication

insights.claim: Because both superconducting and silicon-spin qubits rely on advanced semiconductor fabrication, HRL's technology lets IBM share learning cycles across manufacturing, control electronics, and cryogenics rather than running two disconnected programs.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Shared fab and cryo infrastructure is what makes a two-modality strategy affordable — the cost argument for why this deal is not just optionality.
insights.quote: Because both modalities rely on advanced semiconductor fabrication techniques, the addition of HRL’s technology enables shared learning cycles across manufacturing, control electronics, and cryogenics.
insights.locator: Adding a Dual-Track Modality via Silicon Fabrication

insights.claim: HRL brings a history in semiconductor quantum dot engineering including demonstrations of digitally controlled silicon processing units built on standard CMOS-compatible processes.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: CMOS compatibility is the scaling argument for spin qubits — it opens the possibility of leveraging existing foundry capacity rather than bespoke fabs.

insights.claim: The transaction creates opportunities for HRL to collaborate with Anderon, the pure-play quantum wafer foundry IBM established in May 2026 with U.S. Department of Commerce support.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Government-backed quantum foundry capacity plus in-house spin-qubit IP is a vertical stack competitors would have to replicate at high capital cost.

insights.claim: HRL's portfolio extends beyond qubits to ultra-precise quantum sensors for defense, navigation, and life sciences, plus research into novel quantum materials for high-efficiency detectors and chips.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: The sensing and materials assets give IBM a defense-adjacent revenue option that is commercially closer than fault-tolerant computing.

insights.claim: IBM remains on track to deploy its Starling system by 2029, described as capable of 100 million quantum operations, followed by Blue Jay in the mid-2030s projected at 1 billion operations.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: These are IBM's checkable public milestones — the dates and operation counts against which every quantum sector narrative should be scored.
insights.quote: IBM remains on track to deploy its Starling system by 2029 (capable of 100 million quantum operations), followed by Blue Jay in the mid-2030s (projected for 1 billion operations).

insights.claim: IBM positions the HRL capabilities as an additional technology track for the phase when systems scale toward millions of physical qubits, implying spin qubits matter after, not during, the Starling/Blue Jay era.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Sets expectations: this acquisition is a 2030s payoff, so near-term IBM quantum revenue still rides entirely on the superconducting roadmap.
insights.quote: Integrating HRL’s hardware capabilities provides an additional technology track as systems scale toward millions of physical qubits.
insights.locator: The deal supports IBM’s multi-decade vision
